strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General because no contribution type is declared. The paper introduces a technically interesting computational-imaging method that combines patch-conditioned diffusion with full-image, PSF-based guidance and per-patch scale estimation.

The proposed minimalist imaging setting—recovering 31 spectral bands from a same-resolution grayscale measurement using a single phase-only optic—is novel and potentially impactful. The method improves substantially over eight retrained baselines on simulated ARAD1K data: 34.63 dB versus 31.77 dB for the next-best method, alongside better SSIM and SAM.

The experimental study is broad and informative. It includes guidance, patch-size, overlap, normalization, runtime, measurement-noise, and eight-PSF ablations, as well as tests on CAVE, ICVL, and Harvard images at resolutions up to 1280×1280 without fine-tuning.

The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and supplies useful architectural, optical-simulation, runtime, and training details. The saliency analysis also provides evidence that the network learns spatial dependencies related to the simulated PSF.

Producing multiple reconstructions and testing whether their variance predicts error is useful. The reported pooled pixel-level Pearson correlation of 0.80 indicates promising uncertainty information.
weaknesses: All measurements are simulated with the same forward model used by the reconstruction guidance. There is no fabricated lens, real sensor capture, measured PSF, or experiment with calibration error. Consequently, the central practical claim is not yet validated against field-dependent PSFs, fabrication tolerances, misalignment, vignetting, sensor response, shot/read noise, saturation, and quantization. Claims about compactness and light efficiency should therefore be framed as prospective.

The comparison does not isolate why the method wins. The proposed method receives expensive test-time physics optimization—20 DDIM steps with 20 guidance iterations—whereas the principal baselines are fixed-resolution feed-forward architectures adapted from other sensing models. A full-image diffusion model, standard optimization or plug-and-play reconstruction, and physics-guided baselines under comparable compute are missing. Thus, the conclusion that local patch processing is better than a larger receptive field is not established by Table 1.

Several definitions are inconsistent or apparently incorrect. Equation (6) normalizes the guidance gradient, but Algorithm 1 does not; the guidance step size and important sampling details are not reported. More seriously, the supplementary SAM formula lacks the square root in the norm product, and the PSNR formula does not clearly square the peak value. These equations must be corrected and the authors should confirm that all tabulated metrics used standard implementations.

The uncertainty evidence is preliminary: it uses only ten samples and reports one correlation pooled over pixels, which may be dominated by variation across images or regions. There are no per-image correlations, calibration or coverage tests, comparisons to uncertainty baselines, or quantitative support for the claim that uncertainty increases appropriately out of distribution.

The title and some conclusions overstate the demonstrated scope. 'Any resolution' is supported only by several simulated sizes under a shift-invariant PSF, while inference still requires full-image stitching, convolution, and memory that scale with image area. Likewise, the claim of capturing 'full spectral information' is too strong for an extremely underdetermined inverse problem whose output necessarily depends heavily on learned natural-image priors.

The robustness study uses additive Gaussian noise and asserts that 20 dB SNR should be readily attainable, but provides no hardware-based justification. A realistic photon/read-noise model and perturbations of the assumed PSF are especially important for judging feasibility. The RGB experiment is also labeled Bayer in the main table even though the primary results assume three separate, spatially uniform color measurements rather than an actual Bayer mosaic.

strengths: The paper studies an important and extremely ill-posed computational-imaging problem, and the combination of patch-conditioned diffusion with full-image measurement-consistency guidance is technically coherent. The manuscript is generally clear and well illustrated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/ec9a0920d9284d2eaada23f4adb7898c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The simulation study is broad: eight reconstruction baselines, multiple PSFs, patch-size and guidance ablations, runtime measurements, synthetic noise experiments, and cross-dataset tests. On ARAD1K, the reported 34.63 dB versus 31.77 dB for the strongest listed baseline is substantial, while Table 2 clearly establishes the importance of guidance and patch rescaling.

The supplement provides useful optical-design equations, architecture details, pseudocode, and quantitative runtime results. Testing eight physically motivated PSFs also connects the reconstruction algorithm to optical design rather than treating the forward operator as arbitrary.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The manuscript nevertheless makes strong Applied/Systems claims about enabling compact, light-efficient cameras, but every measurement is simulated. There is no fabricated lens, captured measurement, calibration experiment, or even validation of the simulated PSF against a physical prototype. This gap is consequential because the headline contribution is a proposed imaging system, not merely reconstruction under an abstract convolution operator.

The forward model omits or idealizes several effects central to feasibility: field-dependent and angle-dependent PSFs, fabrication errors, alignment and calibration mismatch, finite aperture/NA and field of view, sensor quantization and saturation, stray light, and realistic shot/read noise. Only matched additive Gaussian noise is evaluated. Consequently, claims such as “first demonstration,” “full spectral information,” improved light efficiency, and readiness for real-world acquisition are not supported by the presented evidence.

For an Algorithms/General contribution, the algorithmic novelty and comparisons are insufficiently isolated. The method largely combines conditional patch diffusion, established diffusion posterior guidance, and a least-squares patch-scale correction. The eight baselines are predominantly architectures developed for other hyperspectral forward models and are modified for this setting. Missing controls include a full-image version of the same diffusion backbone, closely related patch-diffusion inverse solvers, and diffusion/posterior-sampling baselines using the same forward operator and comparable compute. Thus, the results do not establish whether the gain comes from the claimed patch formulation, diffusion modeling, guidance compute, or unequal model suitability.

The optical evidence is incomplete. The title calls the lens “phase-only,” whereas the simulated nanocylinder response explicitly includes wavelength-dependent transmittance. There is no tolerance analysis, aperture/NA specification, off-axis analysis, comparison with optimized conventional diffractive encoders, or end-to-end optical optimization. Table 3 trains a different reconstruction model for every PSF, so it is also difficult to separate encoder quality from training variation.

The uncertainty experiment demonstrates only a Pearson correlation of 0.80 between ten-sample predictive variance and error on simulated in-distribution data. It does not assess calibration, coverage, selective prediction, stability with sample count, spectral uncertainty, or performance under forward-model mismatch. Correlation alone is inadequate support for the claimed reliability indicator, particularly for a severely underdetermined inverse problem where a learned prior may confidently hallucinate plausible spectra.

Cross-dataset evaluation still applies the same synthetic, perfectly known forward model and therefore does not address the dominant simulation-to-real concern. It provides no comparisons on those datasets. The claimed CAVE discrimination application is qualitative and reports reconstruction metrics rather than an actual classification accuracy or decision protocol.

Important reproducibility details remain ambiguous: the value or schedule of the guidance step size is absent, Eq. 6 uses gradient normalization while Algorithm 1 does not, and the non-iterative solution of the coupled patch-scale problem is not specified. In addition, the main text labels three-channel results as Bayer measurements, but the supplement states that these results effectively assume three sequential captures through uniform filters rather than a true Bayer mosaic; the claimed small true-mosaic degradation is not tabulated.

strengths: The paper presents a compelling Algorithms/General contribution: patch-conditioned diffusion is combined with full-field physics guidance to address an unusually underdetermined grayscale-to-hyperspectral inverse problem. Enforcing optical consistency after stitching patches is technically well motivated and broadly relevant to computational imaging.

The empirical gains are substantial. On simulated filterless ARAD1K measurements, the proposed method reaches 34.63 dB PSNR, 0.94 SSIM, and 0.11 SAM, improving over the strongest reported baseline by 2.86 dB, 0.04 SSIM, and 0.04 SAM. Qualitative results likewise show better spatial detail and spectral profiles.

The evaluation is unusually broad: eight reconstruction baselines, eight optical designs, patch-size and overlap ablations, guidance/runtime analysis, measurement-noise experiments, RGB variants, saliency analysis, and cross-dataset tests on CAVE, ICVL, and Harvard. The strong ablation of guidance—roughly 2.5 dB improvement at the standard setting—supports the central algorithmic claim.

The investigation of optical encoders is valuable in its own right. The results identify a meaningful tradeoff between spectral mixing and spatial blur, with the T4 and R1 designs outperforming both an all-in-focus lens and more dispersive rotating PSFs.

Processing local patches makes the trained model applicable to substantially larger spatial resolutions, and testing native images as large as 1280×1280 provides useful evidence for this scalability claim. The reported cross-dataset results are encouraging despite distribution shift.

Sampling-based uncertainty is a useful addition: its reported Pearson correlation of 0.80 with pixelwise reconstruction error suggests practical value for detecting unreliable regions. The paper is also clear, well organized, visually polished, and supported by a detailed supplement covering optical design, noise robustness, runtime, architecture, and sampling pseudocode. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/53670fe690be49f79b3b2fade0babc73/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The largest limitation is that every measurement is simulated. No fabricated lens, calibrated PSF, or real sensor capture is evaluated, despite claims about enabling a physical camera. Real systems introduce wavelength-dependent efficiency, sensor noise and saturation, PSF calibration error, spatial variance, misalignment, stray light, and manufacturing tolerances. The Gaussian-noise study addresses only a small part of this simulation-to-real gap.

Baseline fairness needs stronger documentation. The proposed method receives repeated physics-guidance optimization and apparently averages ten stochastic reconstructions, whereas the baselines are deterministic feed-forward models. Single-sample results, compute- or runtime-matched comparisons, parameter/training-budget details, and a conventional full-image diffusion baseline would help separate the benefits of patch training, diffusion priors, test-time optimization, and ensembling.

The uncertainty evidence is promising but incomplete. A single pooled Pearson correlation over 12.5K pixels does not establish calibration and may be influenced by between-image difficulty or intensity. Per-image correlations, risk-coverage curves, interval coverage, calibration error, and comparisons to simple ensemble or residual proxies are needed before strong reliability claims.

Several implementation details affecting reproducibility are underspecified or inconsistent. Equation 6 normalizes the guidance gradient, whereas Algorithm 1 does not; it is unclear whether the denoiser/noise estimate is recomputed during each inner guidance iteration; and the exact solution, constraints, conditioning, and cost of the coupled least-squares patch-scaling problem are not given. The guidance step size is also absent from the model summary.

The claim of operation at “any resolution” is somewhat overstated. The experiments demonstrate several larger synthetic resolutions, but do not characterize boundary handling, non-multiples of the patch size, memory scaling, or physical changes in sampling and PSF across sensors. The stated O(n² log n) complexity also warrants empirical scaling results.

Some secondary claims are supported mainly qualitatively. The real-versus-fake-object example uses only five scenes and reports no discrimination accuracy, while the saliency analysis shows association with the PSF but does not establish that the learned representation correctly inverts the image-formation model.

The metric definitions require correction or clarification: the supplementary PSNR expression appears to use a peak value rather than its square, and the normalization and dynamic range used for all reported metrics should be stated precisely. These presentation issues are likely correctable but currently impede exact reproduction.

strengths: This is a strong Applied/Systems contribution combining a novel guided patch-diffusion reconstruction method with a fabricated single-metalens prototype. Treating it as Applied/Systems is more appropriate than the default Algorithms/General category: the physical proof of concept and optical-computational trade-off materially strengthen the contribution.

The inference-time guidance is well motivated: independently denoised patches are stitched and constrained by the full-field optical forward model. Ablations show that guidance improves PSNR from 32.32 to 34.67 dB for 64-pixel patches and is especially valuable when the patch size approaches the PSF support.

The evaluation is unusually broad. It includes comparisons with eight reconstruction networks, multiple simulated PSFs, cross-dataset transfer, noise robustness, patch-size and overlap ablations, CASSI generalization, and an analysis of the homogeneous-region failure mode. The reported 34.63 dB on the filterless ARAD1K setting is 2.86 dB above the next-best baseline.

Fabricating and calibrating the metalens is a substantial validation beyond simulation. On eight held-out tabletop scenes, the system reconstructs 26 spectral channels at 640x960 resolution with average PSNR 31.20 dB, SAM 0.157, and SSIM 0.894.

The paper explicitly acknowledges important limitations, including dependence on spatial texture, inability to recover spectra in homogeneous regions, high inference cost, and lack of global context. The saliency and controlled checkerboard analyses provide useful evidence supporting these observations.

Sampling variance correlates with reconstruction error in both simulation and experiment, with reported Pearson correlations of 0.80 and 0.69. This is a useful secondary capability, although its calibration is not fully established.
weaknesses: The physical validation remains small and lacks quantitative reconstruction baselines. Only eight tabletop test scenes are evaluated, after adaptation on six scenes from the same apparatus, and the experimental section does not report numerical comparisons against unguided reconstruction, conventional regressors, alternative inverse solvers, or another optical design. Thus, the real-system results establish feasibility more convincingly than comparative superiority.

Some central implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The guidance step size eta is not specified; the main equation normalizes the guidance gradient whereas supplementary Algorithm 1 does not; and the number N of stochastic reconstructions used for uncertainty maps is never reported. These omissions impede exact reproduction and obscure the total computational cost of uncertainty estimation.

The baseline comparison is not fully controlled. Competing methods originate from different, generally better-conditioned HSI systems and are described only as receiving 'minimal modifications.' There is no whole-image conditional diffusion baseline or comparably sized patch-regression baseline, making it difficult to isolate gains from diffusion, patch training, model capacity, and substantially more expensive iterative inference.

The experimental reference HSIs come from an adjacent camera and are only approximately registered by per-scene homographies. Since the scenes contain depth variation, residual geometric mismatch can materially affect pixelwise PSNR, SSIM, SAM, spectral plots, and the measured uncertainty-error correlation. Registration uncertainty is not quantified.

The optical advantage is not fully characterized experimentally. The prototype uses an aperture-level 450-700 nm band-pass filter, so 'filterless' should be qualified as lacking a pixelwise spectral filter array. Absolute throughput, exposure, sensor noise, and performance relative to a filtered or conventional-lens camera are not measured; the reported 96% concerns energy within a cropped PSF region rather than end-to-end efficiency.

The uncertainty evidence demonstrates error ranking but not calibrated posterior uncertainty. Pearson correlation alone does not establish coverage or calibration, and the CASSI results obtained after discarding high-uncertainty pixels are selective-risk results rather than directly comparable full-image reconstruction scores.

strengths: The manuscript presents a technically compelling computational-imaging system: a single fabricated metalens and filterless monochrome sensor reconstruct a 26–31-band hyperspectral cube from one grayscale exposure. This is a meaningful and challenging vision contribution, supported by both simulation and a physical prototype. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/b0e907e1a1ee47ffb50dc22bd7d8d637/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than purely Algorithms/General: its strongest contribution is the integration of learned reconstruction, optical design, fabrication, calibration, and real capture. Under that framing, the fabricated prototype and measured-PSF evaluation materially strengthen the case for acceptance.

The proposed global physical-consistency guidance addresses a real weakness of independent patch reconstruction when the PSF support approaches or exceeds the patch size. The ablations support this mechanism: guidance improves the main 64-pixel model from 32.2 to 34.7 dB and has an even larger effect for 32-pixel patches.

The simulation evaluation is broad. On ARAD1K the method reports 34.6 dB, compared with 31.8 dB for the strongest listed baseline, and also improves SAM and SSIM. The paper additionally examines eight PSFs, patch size, overlap, normalization, guidance iterations, noise robustness, cross-dataset transfer, and transfer to CASSI.

The real-system results are substantial for a proof of concept: eight held-out tabletop scenes are reconstructed at 640×960×26 with average PSNR 31.20 dB, SAM 0.157, and SSIM 0.894. The paper also discloses the important failure mode on homogeneous regions and provides a controlled checkerboard analysis.

The uncertainty signal is potentially valuable: sample variance correlates with reconstruction error in simulation and experiment, with reported Pearson correlations of 0.80 and 0.69, respectively. The presentation is generally clear, visually informative, and unusually thorough.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not fully controlled. Most baselines were designed for better-conditioned CASSI or RGB settings and are adapted to this new operator, whereas the proposed method uses expensive iterative diffusion guidance. The feed-forward UNet regression ablation does not isolate the effects of patching, diffusion training, and inference-time optimization. A matched full-image diffusion/posterior-sampling baseline, or a patch model with comparable iterative optimization, is needed to substantiate the claim that patch diffusion itself is responsible for the gain.

Real-data validation remains narrow and lacks competing reconstruction methods. It covers only eight indoor tabletop scenes from one device and setup, after LoRA adaptation on six related scenes. There is no real-measurement comparison against adapted baselines, no evaluation under new illumination or depth regimes, and no independent spectral-instrument validation beyond the adjacent reference camera. Thus the prototype establishes feasibility more convincingly than broad practical robustness.

The physical ground truth is only approximately registered using a homography between adjacent cameras, even for depth-varying scenes. Training deliberately models this misalignment, but residual registration errors can still distort PSNR, SSIM, spectral curves, and uncertainty-error correlations. The manuscript does not quantify registration error or provide an evaluation restricted to accurately aligned planar targets.

The claimed uncertainty is evaluated mainly through correlation with squared error. This does not demonstrate probabilistic calibration, interval coverage, or reliable behavior under distribution shift. Moreover, the number of stochastic samples N and sampling stochasticity are not specified, making the uncertainty results difficult to reproduce and their computational cost unclear.

Several important reproducibility details are missing or inconsistent: the guidance step size eta is unspecified; the main normalized-gradient equation and supplementary pseudocode differ; the stochastic DDIM settings and total training iterations are not reported; and the manuscript states that 15 additional scenes were captured but accounts for only six finetuning and eight test scenes. No code, trained model, optical design files, or capture data release is stated.

The method is computationally heavy—approximately 13 minutes for a real 640×960 scene and up to 52 minutes on larger datasets—and its fundamental inability to recover spectra in homogeneous regions limits applicability. These limitations are candidly acknowledged, but they weaken claims of a generally practical snapshot hyperspectral camera. Overall, the contribution supports acceptance, though the missing matched baselines, limited real evaluation, and reproducibility gaps justify a weak-accept rather than an unqualified accept.

strengths: The paper makes a compelling Applied/Systems contribution, combining a fabricated single-metalens, filterless snapshot camera with a guided patch-diffusion reconstruction method. This framing is more appropriate than judging it solely as a new reconstruction algorithm, and the successful physical prototype substantially strengthens the case for acceptance.

The proposed inference procedure is technically well motivated: independently denoised patches are synchronized through a differentiable full-image optical-consistency loss, while least-squares patch rescaling addresses an otherwise important normalization ambiguity. Ablations show that guidance improves PSNR from 32.32 to 34.6 dB and is especially valuable when the patch size approaches the PSF support.

The experimental evidence is broad and generally convincing. On simulated filterless ARAD1K measurements, the method improves over the strongest reported baseline by approximately 2.8 dB while also improving SSIM and SAM. Cross-dataset tests on ICVL, Harvard, and CAVE, experiments with eight PSF designs, noise tests, CASSI results, and high-resolution reconstructions support both effectiveness and scalability.

The fabricated-prototype evaluation is a major strength. The authors measure and calibrate the physical PSF, validate approximate shift invariance, account for sim-to-real discrepancies, and report results on eight held-out tabletop scenes with no objects shared with the six finetuning scenes. The achieved average of 31.20 dB PSNR, 0.894 SSIM, and 0.157 SAM is credible evidence of feasibility rather than a simulation-only demonstration.

Sampling variability is put to practical use as a spatial reliability indicator. The reported uncertainty-error correlations of 0.80 in simulation and 0.69 on physical data, including per-wavelength analysis, are promising and unusually useful for an ill-posed computational-imaging system.

The manuscript is clear, visually effective, and unusually candid about runtime and failure modes. In particular, it explicitly identifies the fundamental ambiguity in large homogeneous regions and supports that limitation with a controlled checkerboard experiment.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation remains small and narrow: it contains only eight held-out indoor tabletop scenes from one prototype, sensor, optical configuration, and approximate field of view. More varied illumination, depth, outdoor content, and independent physical setups would be needed to substantiate broad practical robustness.

Physical evaluation lacks comparisons against alternative reconstruction methods on the same captured measurements. Although adapting existing methods to this unusual forward model is nontrivial and simulation comparisons are extensive, experimental baseline results would help separate the benefit of guided diffusion from calibration, finetuning, and the optical design.

The reference HSIs and prototype measurements are captured by adjacent cameras and aligned with a single homography despite depth variation. Random-offset training is a reasonable mitigation, but residual registration error can affect both quantitative metrics and LoRA supervision. A quantitative registration-error analysis or evaluation on precisely aligned planar targets would make the reported physical accuracy more secure.

The uncertainty analysis establishes correlation with squared error but not probabilistic calibration. Coverage-versus-confidence curves, calibration error, comparison to simpler uncertainty proxies, and explicit reporting of the number of samples and added inference cost would be needed to justify stronger uncertainty-quantification claims.

Inference is expensive: reconstruction takes about 13 minutes for a 640x960 experimental crop and as much as 52 minutes for higher-resolution simulated scenes on an RTX 3090. This is acceptable for a feasibility-oriented computational-imaging contribution, but it substantially limits deployment and the suggested distillation route is not experimentally demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of an explicit code, trained-model, optical-design, calibration-data, or captured-dataset release commitment. There are also minor specification inconsistencies: the main equation normalizes the guidance gradient whereas the supplementary pseudocode does not, and the stated 15 captured scenes do not transparently reconcile with six finetuning plus eight test scenes. These points appear fixable but should be clarified.
